places.history_en: Residents of the new market street raised money for this temple in 1856 and finished it in 1859. It is small, about 46 ping (roughly 152 square metres), and has stayed on the same spot on Dihua Street ever since. The main god is the Xia-Hai City God. A City God's Wife was added in 1893, and a statue of the Old Man under the Moon, the matchmaker god, arrived in 1971 and is now the most visited. The temple became a city monument on 19 August 1985. A 1994-1998 restoration was dedicated on 16 May 1998.
places.history_zh: 咸豐六年（1856）集資興建，1859年落成，廟地僅約46坪。主祀霞海城隍，1893年增祀城隍夫人，1971年供奉月下老人，求姻緣者眾。1985年8月19日指定為市定古蹟，1998年整修完成。

places.years: market founded 1908; current building reopened 1985 (one source); still open
places.history_en: The market began in 1908 under Japanese rule as a public food market for the Yongle-cho district. Japanese traders brought printed cloth in through Dadaocheng, and the market slowly turned into the main fabric wholesale centre of Taiwan. One source says the old market was torn down in 1982 and reopened on the same site in 1985 as a multi-storey building. Fresh food is on the ground floor, fabric stalls on the floors above, and since 2010 the Dadaocheng Theatre has used the 8th and 9th floors.

places.years: renamed 31 Oct 2009; trial opening 6 Mar 2010; still open
places.history_en: The top floors of the Yongle Market building were a district activity centre from February 1987. The space was rebuilt from March 2009 as part of a city plan to revive old Dadaocheng, renamed Dadaocheng Theatre on 31 October 2009, and began trial operation on 6 March 2010. The 9th floor holds a 506-seat theatre for Taiwanese opera, Peking opera, Nanguan, Beiguan and Hakka opera. The 8th floor has a small hall of about 100 seats for glove puppetry and storytelling, plus a corridor exhibition on three puppet traditions. It is run by the Taipei Arts Promotion Office.

places.years: street formed 1850s; named Dihua Street 1947; 77 historic buildings kept under the 1995 plan
places.history_en: Dihua Street took shape in the 1850s and by the late 1800s was Taipei's main street for dried goods, tea, Chinese medicine and cloth. In the Qing era it was several short streets, such as South Street, Middle Street and Middle-North Street. Under Japan it was Yongle-cho; in 1947 it was renamed after Dihua, today's Urumqi. Four facade types stand side by side: low Minnan houses, two-storey Western-style houses, Baroque-style fronts with raised sculpted gables, and plain Modernist fronts, the most common type. A 1995 plan kept the street at its old width and preserved 77 historic buildings.
places.history_zh: 迪化街成形於咸豐年間，清末為南北貨、茶葉、中藥與布匹集散地，1947年定名。街屋立面可分閩南式、洋樓式、仿巴洛克式與現代主義式四類。1995年確定維持原路寬，保存77棟歷史性建築。

places.years: Watsons trading here from 1917 (another source says about 1928); listed 2005; ArtYard from 2011
places.history_en: This corner building carried the Watsons name as a wholesaler of imported Western medicine on Dihua Street from 1917, though one account puts the opening at about 1928. A travel article calls it the first Western pharmacy in Taiwan and, in its day, the tallest and grandest building nearby. The old shop was listed as a Taipei city monument in 2005. In 2011 part of it became ArtYard, a shared house of small culture businesses, with a bookshop about the 1920s on the ground floor, a cafe, and a small theatre on the third floor.

places.years: trade port from the 1860s; revived as a leisure wharf 2005; still open
places.history_en: After Tamsui opened as a treaty port in 1860, Dadaocheng passed Monga as the trading centre of northern Taiwan, and foreign firms shipped tea, sugar and camphor from this riverbank. The wharf faded as river trade declined. In 2005 the Taipei City Government revived it as a place for tourism, cycling and boat trips on the Tamsui River. Boats leave for Tamsui, and a container market with food, coffee and craft beer stands outside Flood Gate No. 5. The riverside park beside it hosts the summer fireworks.

places.years: built 1934; tea trade wound down after the 1960s; restored 2015; open to the public 20 Sep 2016
places.history_en: Tea merchant Wang Fang-qun came from Anxi in Fujian, and his son Wang Lian-he built this tea house in 1934. The ground floor was shop and workshop, the second floor offices and a reception room, and the third floor a shrine hall and family rooms. Business faded after the 1960s. The building was registered as a historic building on 8 March 2005 and approved as a city monument in 2009. A four-year restoration ended with a ceremony on 18 December 2015, the TV drama Purple Dadaocheng filmed here, and it opened to the public on 20 September 2016.

places.history_en: Liao Shui-lai, who had trained at a Japanese-run Western restaurant, opened Bolero in 1934 and named it after Ravel's music. It had some of the best sound equipment in Taiwan and played imported classical records, so young writers and artists met here to listen and talk. Painter Yan Yun-lian redesigned the interior in 1947. The house dishes are country-style curry rice and French duck rice, served on steel plates made for the shop. In 1976 the second generation split the business, and a second Bolero opened a few doors away at No. 308.

places.en: Lin Wu-hu Hall (Lin family old house)
places.years: built 1851; still standing, run as a fortune-telling hall
places.history_en: In 1851 the merchant Lin Lan-tian moved from Keelung to Dadaocheng to get away from pirates and built three shophouses here. They are counted among the oldest buildings on Dihua Street and are called its first Minnan-style shophouse. The plan is three halls with two courtyards between them. The front hall on the street was for trade, the middle hall with its open well was for family life and guests, and the back hall was a warehouse that once opened toward the Tamsui River. The family repairs it about every ten years. Today it houses the Lin Wu-hu fortune-telling hall.
places.history_zh: 咸豐元年（1851）商人林藍田自基隆遷來所建，為迪化街最古老的閩南式街屋之一。三進兩院：前進營商、中進設樓井為起居空間、後進為倉庫，昔日可通淡水河。現為林五湖命相館。

places.en: Dadaocheng Cisheng Temple (Mazu temple and food court)
places.years: first built 1864; moved 1866 and 1910; current temple completed 1914; still open
places.history_en: This Mazu temple was first built in 1864 and moved in 1866 to a site facing the Dadaocheng wharf. Japanese-era street planning forced another move in 1910, and the temple was rebuilt on its present site by 1914 using the old materials. Its stone dragon columns, tablets and carved beams were shipped from Xiamen and cut by craftsmen from Tong'an. The forecourt is lined with old food stalls selling pork rib soup, fried rice with whitebait, smoked shark, Shantou buns and four-herb soup. It was made a city monument on 22 December 2020.
places.history_zh: 主祀媽祖，同治三年（1864）創建，1866年遷至面向碼頭處，1910年因市區改正再遷，1914年於現址重建完成，石柱雕樑沿用舊材。廟埕小吃攤林立，有排骨湯、魩仔魚炒飯、鯊魚煙等。2020年指定為市定古蹟。

places.years: house rebuilt about 1932; Li died here 13 Feb 1979; opened to the public 26 Jul 2024
places.history_en: Li Lin-qiu was a lyricist, linked above all with the song Bang Chhun Hong (望春風). He lived and wrote in this house from middle age until he died here on 13 February 1979. The plot was first built on about 1887, and around 1932 it was rebuilt as a two-storey brick shophouse. The front is only about 5.4 metres wide, with four columns making three bays. The city listed it as a monument (the page gives both 27 December 2021 and 21 February 2022), and after restoration it opened as an arts space on 26 July 2024.

places.en: Lin Liu-hsin Puppet Theatre Museum (Taiyuan Asian Puppet Theatre Museum)
places.history_en: The museum opened in 2000 as the TTT Puppet Centre. In November 2005 it was renamed the Lin Liu-hsin Puppet Theatre Museum, and later the Taiyuan Asian Puppet Theatre Museum. Its founder, Dr Lin Jing-fu, began collecting after seeing a fine traditional puppet on a trip to Japan in the 1990s. The collection grew to more than 10,000 pieces from around the world: glove puppets, shadow puppets, string puppets and water puppets. It also ran workshops and shows. The museum closed on 1 July 2019, so it fits the 2000-2019 scene almost exactly.

places.history_en: Zhan Tian-ma, a well-known silent-film narrator, opened this tea house in 1941 in the Taihei-cho part of Dadaocheng. On 27 February 1947 Monopoly Bureau inspectors seized the cigarettes of a widow selling in front of it, and the shooting that followed set off the 228 Incident. The old building was pulled down at the end of 2005 and a taller block replaced it. Local elders and culture workers reopened a tea house on the third floor of the new building in 2011. A plaque in Chinese and English marks the flash point a little to the east.

A travel write-up says it was founded in 1894 and is now run by the fourth generation, and that the family first sold red turtle cakes, herb cakes and other pastries before oil rice became the main item. events.en: Dihua Street Lunar New Year Market
events.years: first held 1996; yearly before Lunar New Year; 2026 edition 31 Jan to 15 Feb
events.history_en: For about two weeks before Lunar New Year, Dihua Street turns into Taipei's best-known holiday market. It began in 1996 and was the first of its kind in Taiwan. Shops push stalls into the arcades, hand out samples and shout prices over the crowd, and more than a million people come. The 2026 edition ran from 31 January to 15 February, noon to midnight, with photo spots built around popular cartoon characters. Young people come for the snacks, the samples and the photos.

events.zh: 霞海城隍聖誕遶境（五月十三迎城隍）
events.years: 13th day of the 5th lunar month, yearly; earliest record 1879; resumed 1898
events.history_en: Every year on the 13th day of the fifth lunar month, the City God leaves his small temple on Dihua Street and is carried around Dadaocheng with a parade of temple troupes. The earliest record is from 1879; it was banned early in Japanese rule and came back in 1898 after an epidemic. The crowd is so thick that the saying goes: on the thirteenth, people come to watch people. Young visitors join for the street spectacle and the photos.

events.years: first year (unknown — needs CJ); running by 2006; yearly around Qixi; 2026 edition 25 Jul to 15 Aug
events.history_en: Each summer near Qixi, the Chinese Valentine's Day, fireworks go up over the Tamsui River beside Dadaocheng Wharf. The show was already running in 2006, with about 7,000 shells. Today it is the Dadaocheng Summer Festival. The 2026 edition opened on 25 July with its first drone light show, a Spider-Man theme and a nine-metre Spider-Man at the wharf, plus live sets by acts such as Bennu, and ran until 15 August. It is the classic Taipei summer date night.

events.years: first held 2015 (inferred); yearly in October; 2025 parade on 12 October
events.history_en: Every October the Tua-Tiu-Tiann International Festival of Arts fills Dadaocheng with plays, music and dance for about a month. Its highlight is the 1920s costume parade. In 2025, on 12 October, people dressed as 1920s gentry, ladies and street vendors set off on five routes and met at the Yongle Plaza main stage, where the day ended with a starlit ball. Young people come to dress up, take photos and dance in the street.

events.history_en: In season 5 of the Japanese drama Solitary Gourmet (孤獨的美食家), episodes 4 and 5 sent the hero Goro to Taiwan, the show's first trip abroad. Goro, played by Yutaka Matsushige (松重豐), ate at Yongle Danzai Noodles beside Yongle Market. The shop still sells a Goro set, a chicken rice box with side dishes. Fans from Japan and Taiwan come to eat exactly what he ate, and Matsushige has come back to Taiwan to film again since.

events.history_en: PIER5 opened on 1 April 2018 inside flood gate 5 at Dadaocheng Wharf, at the river end of Minsheng West Road. White shipping containers were turned into small food and drink bars beside the Tamsui River, and the place quickly became a photo spot that drew big crowds. The organiser planned themed markets on two weekends a month and regular sets by singer-songwriters and bands. Young people come in the evening for a drink, the river breeze and live music.

events.en: Matchmaker-god crowds at Xia-Hai City God Temple
events.years: Yue Lao worshipped here since 1971; viral Japanese school-trip video October 2025
events.history_en: The Old Man under the Moon, the matchmaker god, has been worshipped at Xia-Hai City God Temple since 1971 and is now the temple's most popular god. Single people come to ask him for a partner. In October 2025 a Threads video of Japanese high-school girls in uniform crowding the temple and its arcade went viral. People joked that the temple had become a stop on Japanese school trips and that the matchmaker now has overseas business.

events_old_history.en: I Love Dihua Street preservation movement
events_old_history.years: widening planned 1973, approved Oct 1977; campaign July 1988; preservation plan 1995
events_old_history.history_en: In the 1970s the city planned to widen Dihua Street from under 8 metres to 20 metres, which would have cut the fronts off its old shophouses. The plan was approved in October 1977. When land was about to be taken in 1988, the Leshan Cultural Foundation started the I Love Dihua Street campaign in July with residents, citizens and scholars, and collected signatures. The widening was paused and universities were asked to study how to save the street. In 1995 a plan fixed the street at its old width and protected 77 historic buildings. Everything a visitor sees today exists because of this fight.
events_old_history.history_zh: 1977年10月市府核定將迪化街拓寬為20公尺，老街屋面臨拆除。1988年7月樂山文教基金會與居民、學者發起「我愛迪化街」連署，拓寬暫緩。1995年確定維持原路寬，保存77棟歷史建築。

events_old_history.zh: 二二八事件引爆點（天馬茶房前緝菸事件）
events_old_history.en: Flash point of the 228 Incident at Tianma Tea House
events_old_history.history_en: On 27 February 1947 six inspectors from the Taipei branch of the Monopoly Bureau caught Lin Jiang-mai, a 40-year-old widow, selling cigarettes in front of Tianma Tea House. They took her goods and money and struck her on the head with a gun butt. As the crowd grew angry, shots were fired; one bystander was killed and another hurt. The next morning people marched south down Dihua Street, east along Nanjing West Road and on to the Monopoly Bureau. The protests spread across Taiwan and were put down by force. This is remembered as the start of the 228 Incident.
events_old_history.history_zh: 1947年2月27日，專賣局臺北分局六名查緝員在天馬茶房前取締寡婦林江邁販菸，以槍托擊傷其頭部，並開槍造成民眾一死一傷。翌日群眾沿迪化街、南京西路遊行抗議，成為二二八事件導火線。

events_old_history.years: fire date (unknown — needs CJ; the brief says 1998); listed as a city monument 2005; ArtYard opened 2011
events_old_history.history_en: The brief for this research names a 1998 fire at the Watsons pharmacy building and its later restoration. None of the pages read confirmed the fire, its date, the damage or the restoration years, so those stay open. What was confirmed: Watsons traded on Dihua Street from 1917, a magazine piece calls the present building a rebuilt Li family house, the old shop was listed as a city monument in 2005, and in 2011 part of it became ArtYard. Do not publish the fire story until a heritage record is read. (unknown — needs CJ)
